title: The Leader-Ship of Theseus
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Using the Ship of Theseus as a frame, Brien asks what happens to a school's culture when its own leaders resist the shared mission. He argues that leaders' behaviour sets the culture, and that quiet resistance from colleagues, including other leaders, can undo otherwise strong instructional practice. Excuses such as our students just are not academic act as a get-out clause that blocks change. His prescription pairs trust with accountability: quietly challenge using a surplus model rather than accusation, listen first, watch for non-apologies and closed-circle arguments, keep paper trails, and hire carefully. The through-line is that everyone must be held to the same standard, because the behaviour leaders walk past is the behaviour they accept.
points: Leaders' conduct shapes school culture more than words, and one misaligned leader can undo otherwise strong practice.
Staff resistance often shows up as undermining comments, withheld resources and avoided meetings, and low expectations of students are a common cover.
Trust and accountability must go together, since trust without accountability is naivety.
Challenge colleagues with a surplus model, letting them be heard first, and recognise non-apologies and closed-circle arguments as warning signs.
Written records and careful hiring give accountability teeth, and the same standard must apply to everyone.
quotes: The behaviour of leaders matters so much to the culture of a school. I previously have left schools where I did not feel supported by one or multiple members of leadership.

This can act magnetically to attract anyone who did not fully agree the school priorities and suddenly create a quiet but powerful resistance to change. This resistance can come in many forms such as; undermining comments on key school priorities publicly, not sharing curriculum documentation or resources, disengaged behaviour in staff meetings and avoiding meetings where possible.
Students will meet the bar you set for them. If you place the bar on the ground they will get a shovel and start digging.
We need trust without building complacency. We need accountability without micromanaging.
What is most important here is that the staff member feels heard. They’ll likely be completely cemented in their ways until they’re able to get all of their thoughts and fears off of their chest.
A closed circle argument is one where there is no possibility of convincing an opponent that they might be wrong. They are right because they’re right.
The overriding point in all of this is that we must hold everybody to the same standards. No one is beyond reproach.
